content: Defecation is the physiological process by which organisms expel solid or semisolid waste material, known as feces, from the digestive tract through the anus. In humans, the frequency of defecation varies widely, ranging from several times a day to a few times per week. In contrast, certain animals, such as sloths, may defecate as infrequently as once a week. The movement of fecal matter through the digestive tract is facilitated by waves of muscular contractions called peristalsis, which occur in the walls of the colon. This process propels the waste material toward the rectum. Occasionally, undigested food may also be expelled in this manner, a process referred to as egestion. The rectal ampulla, also known anatomically as the ampulla recti, serves as a temporary storage site for this waste material. As the rectum fills with fecal matter, its walls expand, activating stretch receptors within the rectal walls that are part of the nervous system. These receptors signal the urge to defecate. If this urge is not acted upon, the material in the rectum may be returned to the colon, where additional water is absorbed. Prolonged delays in defecation can lead to the hardening of fecal matter, resulting in constipation. When the rectum becomes sufficiently full, the increase in intrarectal pressure forces the walls of the anal canal apart, allowing fecal matter to enter the canal. The rectum shortens as the material is pushed into the anal canal, and peristaltic waves facilitate the expulsion of feces. The internal and external anal sphincters play a critical role in this process, allowing the passage of feces by coordinating muscle contractions that pull the anus upward over the exiting material. During defecation, several muscle groups, including the chest muscles, diaphragm, abdominal wall muscles, and pelvic diaphragm, exert pressure on the digestive tract. Simultaneously, ventilation temporarily ceases as the lungs push the chest diaphragm downward to increase pressure. This process causes a rise in blood pressure throughout the body and a temporary decrease in the amount of blood pumped by the heart. These physiological changes resemble the stresses experienced during a Valsalva maneuver. In rare cases, defecation can lead to fatal outcomes if the associated rise in blood pressure causes the rupture of an aneurysm or dislodges blood clots, potentially resulting in thrombosis. The act of defecation requires conscious relaxation of the external anal sphincter muscles to expel waste. The anal and urethral sphincter muscles are closely linked, as demonstrated by research conducted by Dr. Harrison Weed at The Ohio State University Medical Center. His experiments revealed that these sphincters can only contract together and not independently. Both sphincters also exhibit relaxation during urination, which explains why defecation is often accompanied by urination. Defecation can occur either involuntarily or under voluntary control. Young children acquire voluntary control over this process through toilet training. Once trained, loss of control, resulting in fecal incontinence, may occur due to various factors, including physical injury (e.g., damage to the anal sphincter during an episiotomy), intense fear, inflammatory bowel disease, impaired water absorption in the colon (as seen in diarrhea), or psychological and neurological conditions. The positions and methods used for defecation vary across cultures. In regions such as South Asia, East Asia, and rural parts of the Middle East, squatting (often using squat toilets) is customary. In contrast, most of the Western world utilizes sit-down toilets. After defecation, the anus and buttocks may be cleansed using toilet paper or similar paper products. In some cultures, water is used for cleansing, either manually or with devices such as bidets. In Japan, advanced toilets known as washlets are designed to wash and dry the user's anus after defecation.
